comment: Broad feedback: Align the approach more closely with the NHWA framework rather than focusing solely on registries. Health workforce data originate from multiple sources, including HR and payroll systems, professional registers, education systems, censuses, labour force surveys, and sources outside the health sector such as national statistical offices, ministries of finance and higher education, and private institutions. Adopt a comprehensive workforce perspective. The architecture should support data on workforce numbers, distribution, skills, education, inflows and outflows, employment, and future workforce needs—not only registration data. As emphasized in our NHWA training, priority challenges should guide how data are selected and organized. Strengthen the focus on data quality and multi-source integration. The role of triangulation(key to HWF data) should be made more explicit, highlighting the need to combine and validate information from different sources rather than relying on a single system. The architecture should also recognize the importance of analytical and evidence-generation capacities, involving HRH experts and analysts alongside IT specialists. Reinforce governance arrangements, particularly incentives and safeguards for data sharing and data privacy/confidentiality. Private-sector, military, and other stakeholders may require clear benefits, protections, sustainable financing, and differentiated access arrangements before they can contribute data and participate in the architecture. References: NHWA Handbook, [who.int/publications-detail-redirect/national-health-workforce-accounts-implementation-guide]NHWA implementation guide, HWF occupational mapping, HWF terminology
